gap: No result ChatGPT got states a power draw that a reviewer actually measured. LANOC measured the QNAP TS-233 at 3.7 W idle, 5.7 W streaming to Plex and 7.4 W copying files with two SATA SSDs. PC-Welt measured the Synology DS223j at 16.4 W idle, 3.1 W asleep and 22.3 W under load, so the DS223j idles at more than four times the TS-233's measured idle.
standout_why: ChatGPT's cited pages carry only maker figures. The two Synology compare pages list DS124 10.69/3.44 W and DS223j 16.31/4 W as Synology's own numbers, name no reviewer and don't describe the test setup. QNAP's TS-233 spec page lists 10.81 W typical and 3.43 W disk standby, 'tested with drives fully populated', with no method given. ChatGPT's answer itself says its figures are 'manufacturer-published'. None of these pages has a third-party measurement. The reviews in the top results for the TS-233 (StorageReview, NASCompares) only repeat QNAP's 3.43/10.81 W and measured nothing themselves.
decides: This backs up the TS-233 as the 12 V pick and gives a real number for it. With SSDs, LANOC measured 3.7 W idle, about 7 Ah a day from a 12.8 V battery, against QNAP's 10.81 W 'typical', about 20 Ah a day. PC-Welt's DS223j idle of 16.4 W, about 31 Ah a day, matches Synology's 16.31 W access figure. So the Synology 2-bay units cost roughly four times as much battery as an SSD-filled TS-233 while awake. Both draw about 3 W asleep. The comparison isn't like for like: LANOC used SSDs, PC-Welt doesn't name its drives, and neither describes its meter setup. The page should say so.

findings.label: Measured draw: idle / Plex streaming / file transfer
findings.note: Two 500 GB SATA SSDs installed, so there was no disk spin-down. The review doesn't say which meter was used or whether it read at the wall; the author mentions a Sense home energy monitor. The page is dated '08.Jul' with no year; the image paths suggest 2022. At 12.8 V: 3.7 W × 24 h = 88.8 Wh = about 6.9 Ah a day; 7.4 W × 24 h = 177.6 Wh = about 13.9 Ah a day.
